content: When co-administering zuranolone with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, the dose of zuranolone should be reduced. Clinical observations have reported the following adverse effects: elevated liver enzymes (ALT/AST > 5x ULN in 3% of cases), ocular icterus (65% for all grades, 3% for grades 2-4), jaundice (13% for all grades, 5% for grades 2-4), nausea (12% for all grades, 2% for grades 2-4), rash (5% for grades 2-4), elevated creatinine kinase (>10x ULN in 5%), elevated serum amylase (>2x ULN in 4%), glycosuria (≥1000 mcg/dL in 3%), hematuria (>75 RBC/HPF in 3%), and elevated GGT (>5x ULN in 2%). Other reported conditions include nephrolithiasis (2%), gastrointestinal disorders such as diarrhea, vomiting, and upper abdominal pain (<2%), fatigue (<2%), rhabdomyolysis (<2%), headache (<2%), psychiatric disorders like depression, abnormal dreams, and insomnia (<2%), and renal disorders such as nephropathy and Fanconi syndrome (<2%). Patients with a history of clinically significant hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, or toxic skin eruptions) should avoid this medication. Co-administration with drugs highly dependent on CYP3A or UGT1A1 for clearance, or those that strongly induce CYP3A, may lead to significant drug interactions, reduced efficacy, or increased toxicity. Atazanavir, a component of some regimens, has been shown to prolong the PR interval on ECG, with most cases being asymptomatic and limited to first-degree AV block. Rare cases of second-degree AV block and other conduction abnormalities have been reported. Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, toxic skin eruptions, and drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome have been observed. Mild-to-moderate maculopapular skin eruptions were also reported in clinical trials, typically not requiring treatment discontinuation. Atazanavir can cause asymptomatic elevations in indirect bilirubin due to UGT inhibition. Chronic kidney disease has been reported in HIV-infected patients treated with atazanavir, with or without ritonavir. Renal function should be assessed before initiating therapy and monitored during treatment, especially in patients at high risk for renal disease. Cases of nephrolithiasis and/or cholelithiasis have been reported during postmarketing surveillance of atazanavir. Patients with hepatitis B or C infections or elevated transaminases may have an increased risk of further liver enzyme elevations or hepatic decompensation. New-onset diabetes mellitus, exacerbation of preexisting diabetes, and hyperglycemia have been reported in patients receiving protease inhibitors. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a cushingoid appearance, has been observed in patients on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination ART, potentially leading to inflammatory responses to opportunistic infections such as Mycobacterium avium, CMV, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), or tuberculosis. Autoimmune disorders, including Graves' disease, polymyositis, autoimmune hepatitis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported. Increased bleeding, including spontaneous skin hematomas and hemarthrosis, has been observed in patients with hemophilia A and B treated with HIV protease inhibitors. Lactic acidosis syndrome, sometimes fatal, and symptomatic hyperlactatemia have occurred in pregnant women using atazanavir with nucleoside analogues, which are associated with an increased risk of lactic acidosis. Hyperbilirubinemia is common in patients taking atazanavir, including pregnant women. All infants, including neonates exposed to atazanavir in utero, should be monitored for severe hyperbilirubinemia during the first few days of life. Atazanavir is not recommended for use during pregnancy and should not be initiated in pregnant individuals. Alternative regimens are advised for those who become pregnant during therapy. Components of the drug combination may interact with certain oral contraceptives, and nonhormonal contraceptive methods should be considered. The CDC advises HIV-infected mothers in the United States not to breastfeed to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV. It is unknown whether atazanavir or cobicistat is secreted in human milk. Atazanavir should be taken with food. When co-administered with H2-receptor antagonists or proton-pump inhibitors, doses should be separated by at least two hours. Tablets should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with excursions permitted between 15-30°C (59-86°F).
